Tischler and Piet Maes The citation for this ICTV Report chapter is the summary published as: Bradfute, S. B., Calisher, C. H., Klempa, B., Klingström, J., Kuhn, J. H., Laenen, L., Tischler, N. D., & Maes, P. (2024). ICTV Virus Taxonomy Profile: Hantaviridae 2024, Journal of General Virology 105, 001975 Corresponding author: Piet Maes ( [email protected] ) Edited by: Holly Hughes and Evelien Adriaenssens Posted: March 2024, updated June 2024 Summary Hantaviridae is a family for negative-sense RNA viruses with genomes of about 10.5–14.6 kb (Table 1 Hantaviridae ). The family includes eight genera ( Actinovirus and Percilovirus (subfamily Actantavirinae ), Agnathovirus (subfamily Agantavirinae ), Loanvirus , Mobatvirus , Orthohantavirus and Thottimvirus (subfamily Mammantavirinae ), and Reptillovirus (subfamily Repantavirinae ). These viruses are maintained in and/or transmitted by small mammals, but also by fish and reptiles. Several orthohantaviruses can infect humans, causing mild, severe, and sometimes-fatal diseases. Hantavirids produce enveloped virions containing three single-stranded RNA segments with open reading frames (ORFs) that encode a nucleoprotein (N), a glycoprotein precursor (GPC), and large (L) protein containing an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domain. Table 1 Hantaviridae. Characteristics of members of the family Hantaviridae. Characteristic Description* Example Hantaan virus (S segment: M14626; M segment: M14627; L segment: X55901), species Orthohantavirus hantanense Virion Enveloped, pleomorphic virions 80–160 nm in diameter with heterodimeric surface spikes Genome Three single-stranded RNA molecules (segments): small (S; 1.0–3.0 kb), medium (M; 3.4–4.8 kb), and large (L; 5.3–6.8 kb) Replication Ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes containing anti-genomic RNA serve as coding templates for synthesis of genomic RNA Translation Proteins are produced from capped and non-polyadenylated mRNAs. The 5′-cap structure is obtained via cap-snatching from cellular mRNAs Host range Fish (actinoviruses, agnathoviruses, perciloviruses), mammals (orthohantaviruses), and reptiles (reptilloviruses) Taxonomy Realm Riboviria , kingdom Orthornavirae , phylum Negarnaviricota , class Bunyaviricetes , order Elliovirales ; the family includes four subfamilies, eight genera, and 55 species * mostly based on experiments with mammalian orthohantaviruses Viruses assigned to each of the seven genera form genus-specifc monophyletic clades based on phylogenetic analysis of concatenated L protein/RdRP, glycoprotein and N sequences. Viruses from all seven genera share one or more of the following characteristics: (i) enveloped pleomorphic virions; (ii) tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genome without polyadenylated tracts at the 3′-end; (iii) genomic sequence complementarity at the 5′- and 3′-ends; and (iv) capped but not polyadenylated virus mRNAs ( Maes et al., 2004 ). Piscine Hosts Genus Actinovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian (percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) fish. Genus Agnathovirus . Viruses in this genus infect agnathan (myxinid) fish. Genus Percilovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian ( gobiid, lophiid ) fish. Mammalian Hosts Genus Loanvirus. Viruses in this genus infect rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly nycterid bats and possibly murid rodents. Genus Mobatvirus. Viruses in this genus infect emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid and possibly molossid, and vespertillionid bats and soricid and talpid eulipotyphla. Genus Orthohantavirus. Viruses assigned to this genus infect soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Genus Thottimvirus. Viruses in this genus infect soricid and possibly talpid eulipotyphla. Reptilian Hosts Genus Reptillovirus . Viruses in this genus infect gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles. Virion Morphology Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Physicochemical and physical properties Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Nucleic acid Hantavirids have tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genomes (S, M, and L segments). The viral mRNAs are not polyadenylated and contain a 5′-methylated cap and several non-templated nucleotides at the 5′-end that are derived from host cell mRNAs via cap snatching ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Further information is only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Proteins Hantavirids typically express three structural proteins. The most abundant structural protein in a hantavirion is N, which encapsidates the hantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , are produced from GPC and mediate entry of hantavirions ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Spiropoulou 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Lipids Not reported but are likely derived from the Golgi apparatus and/or the host cell plasma membrane and therefore likely composed of phospholipids, glycolipids, fatty acids, and sterols. Carbohydrates Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Genome organization and replication S RNA encodes N and in some viruses NSs ( Jääskeläinen et al., 2007 , Vera-Otarola et al., 2012 ), M RNA encodes GPC, and the L RNA encodes L with its RdRP, helicase, and endonuclease domains ( Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 ) (Figure 1 Hantaviridae ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Figure 1 Hantaviridae . Genome organization of representative hantaviruses. The 5′- and 3′- ends of all segments are complementary at their termini, likely promoting the formation of panhandle RNP complexes within the virion . GPC , glycoprotein precursor gene; L , large (protein) gene; N , nucleoprotein gene. Biology Hantavirids have been found in actinopterygian (gobiid, lophiid, percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) and agnathan (myxinid) fish; in emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid, rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly molossid and nycterid bats; in soricid and talpid eulipotyphla; in muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents; in gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles; and potentially in coleopteran and plectopteran insects (see genus pages for details). Only orthohantaviruses are known to cause diseases (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Antigenicity Systematic antigenicity studies have only been reported for orthohantaviruses (see Orthohantavirus genus page). species demarcation criteria The availability of at least coding-complete sequences of all three genome segments may be sufficient for hantavirid classification in the absence of a cultured isolate. Demarcation of genera is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Hantaviridae: current classification and future perspectives, Viruses, 11, 9, e0788">Laenen et al., 2019 ). DEmARC analysis gave a frequency distribution of Pairwise Evolutionary Distance (PED) values of which the threshold of 0.1 gave an optimal clustering cost of zero and is used as the hantavirid species demarcation criterium. Genera are demarked by a PED-value threshold of 0.95 and subfamilies are demarcated based on their distinct clustering in a Bayesian maximum clade credibility tree and a PED-value threshold of 3.5. Relationships within the family Phylogenetic relationships across the family have been estimated using Bayesian maximum clade credibility trees generated from complete N, GPC, and L amino-acid sequences; similar topologies are obtained with concatenated N and GPC sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Figure 2 Hantaviridae . Maximum likelihood phylogenetic tree inferred using IQ-TREE. The tree was constructed based on 53 concatenated S and M segment (amino acid) sequences using the LG+R9 model of sequence evolution. Branch lengths represent the estimated number of substitutions per site. Bootstrap support values (>70%) are indicated at nodes, reflecting the degree of confidence in the branching pattern. Relationships with other taxa Hantavirids are closely related to bunyaviral crulivirids, fimovirids, peribunyavirids, phasmavirids, tulasvirids, and tospovirids ( Wolf et al., 2018 , Herath et al., 2020 ). Using the Master Species List Using the Virus Metadata Resource Using the Find the Species tool Using the ICTV Report Webinar Webinar on Virus Taxonomy Webinar on Finding Information GitHub Repository Zenodo Repository Email ICTV Help ‏‏‎ ‎ ICTV Report Book: Hantaviridae Family: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Actantavirinae Genus: Actinovirus Genus: Percilovirus Subfamily: Agantavirinae Genus: Agnathovirus Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Loanvirus Genus: Mobatvirus Genus: Orthohantavirus Genus: Thottimvirus Subfamily: Repantavirinae Genus: Reptillovirus Authors: Hantaviridae Citation: Hantaviridae References: Hantaviridae Resources: Hantaviridae Species List: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Orthohantavirus Distinguishing features Sixty different viruses are classified in the genus Orthohantavius. These viruses typically infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease in humans ( Schmaljohn and Hjelle 1997 , Jonsson et al., 2010 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 , Vial et al., 2023 ). Virion Morphology Orthohantavirions are pleomorphic in shape, mostly spherical of 80–160 nm in diameter ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ), and surrounded by a membrane envelope that is decorated with glycoprotein (GP) spikes composed of G N and G C subunits (Figure 1 Orthohantavirus ). The virion envelope is 5 nm thick and is decorated with square shaped spikes, consisting of tetrameric G N -G C heterodimers, which protrude 10 nM from the membrane forming a surface lattice of local symmetry interrupted by empty membrane spots ( Hung et al., 1983 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Parvate et al., 2019 , Serris et al., 2020 , Guardado-Calvo and Rey 2021 ). Isolated ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes are composed of individual segment genomic RNA encapsidated by nucleoprotein (N) ( Tao et al., 1987 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Hepojoki et al., 2012 , Guo et al., 2016 , Arragain et al., 2019 ). Virions assemble and bud from the Golgi complex or cell surface membranes, depending on the virus ( Goldsmith et al., 1995 , Parvate et al., 2019 ). Figure 1 Orthohantavirus. A, B) Electron micrographs of Tula virus particles adapted from ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ). C) Schematic illustration of an orthohantavirus particle. Shown is a spherical and enveloped (grey) particle with glycoprotein spikes (G N yellow, G C blue) inserted in a bilaminar lipid envelope. The S (small), M (medium), and L (large) RNP (ribonucleoprotein) complexes inside the particle consist of N (nucleoprotein, green) and L (large protein, pink). ViralZone image reproduced courtesy of SwissBioPics. Physicochemical and physical properties Virion buoyant densities in sucrose and CsCl are 1.15–1.18 ( White et al., 1982 ) and 1.20–1.21 g cm −3 , respectively ( Schmaljohn et al., 1983 ). Virions are sensitive to chemical inactivation with, for instance, methanol, paraformaldehyde, acetone/methanol, N -ethylmaleimide or detergents, as well as physical methods such as heat, gamma irradiation or UV irradiation ( Kraus et al., 2005 , Strandin et al., 2011 , Elveborg et al., 2022 ). Nucleic acid Orthohantavirus genomes are linear tri-segmented RNA molecules of negative polarity. The genomes are about 11.1–12.3 kb in length (small [S] segment: 1.2–2.1 kb; medium [M] segment: 3.4–3.8 kb; large [L] segment: 6.5–6.6 kb). Proteins Orthohantaviruses typically express three structural proteins (Table 1 Orthohantavirus ). The most abundant structural protein in an orthohantavirion is N, which encapsidates the orthohantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , mediate virion entry. G N and G C and non-structural proteins are encoded as a precursor polyprotein. Table 1 Orthohantavirus . Location and function of orthohantavirus structural proteins. Protein Location, mass, and function Reference Nucleoprotein (N) Structural virion protein (about 48 kD). Oligomerizes and encapsidates orthohantaviral genomic segments and hence component of RNPs. Binds to L and G N ( Mir et al., 2010 , Reuter and Krüger 2018 , Arragain et al., 2019 ) Nonstructural protein (NSs) Non-structural protein encoded by some orhtohantaviruses. Has type I interferon inhibitory activity. May occur as multiple isoforms. ( Vera-Otarola et al., 2020 , Binder et al., 2021 ) Glycoprotein (GP) Structural virion protein consisting of two subunits (G N : about 70-75 kD, G C : about 50-55 kD). Produced via proteolytic cleavage from the genome-encoded precursor GPC. Projects from virion membranes as tetrameric GP spikes composed of G N and G C heterodimers. GP mediates cell- receptor binding; as a class II fusion machine it induces virion-cell membrane fusion and, thereby cell entry. G N binds to N and RNA ( Spiropoulou et al., 2003 , Tischler et al., 2005 , Cifuentes-Muñoz et al., 2014 , Li et al., 2016 , Willensky et al., 2016 , Rissanen et al., 2017 , Zhu et al., 2018 , Bignon et al., 2019 , Sperber et al., 2019 ) Large protein (L) Structural virion protein (246 kD) with RdRP, helicase, and endoribonuclease domains. Component of the RNP inside virions. Binds to N and RNA. Oligomerizes and mediates transcription and replication of viral RNA segments. Mediates cap-snatching for viral mRNA capping. ( Kukkonen et al., 2005 , Cheng et al., 2014 , Rothenberger et al., 2016 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Durieux Trouilleton et al., 2023 ) Genome organization and replication The orthohantavirus genome consists of three negative-sense RNA molecules, termed S (small), M (medium), and L (large) (Figure 2 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 2 Orthohantavirus. Schematic representation of orthohantavirus genome organization. Orthohantavirus genomic segments assume circular forms via non-covalent binding of complementary and highly conserved 3′- and 5′-terminal sequences. Genomic segment reassortment mostly occurs among viruses belonging to the same species but interspecies reassortment likely occurs occasionally ( Klempa 2018 , Petazzi et al., 2021 ). Orthohantavirus infection starts with virion attachment, mediated by G N and G C , to cell-surface attachment factors and entry via the endosomal route ( Shtanko et al., 2014 ) (Figure 3 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 3 Orthohantavirus . Lifecycle of orthohantaviruses. (1) Virion attachment; (2) virion uptake; (3) virion-cell membrane fusion; (4) transcription; (5) translation; (6) replication; (7) virion assembly; and (8) virion egress. After engaging a cellular receptor, protocadherin 1 in the case of American orthohantaviruses, virion-membrane fusion results in early or late endosomal release, depending on the virus, of the virion RNP complex into the cytoplasm in a pH-dependent manner ( Jangra et al., 2018 , Mittler et al., 2019 , Torriani et al., 2019 , Dieterle et al., 2021 ). During primary transcription L generates uncapped antigenomic RNA molecules that are then capped using host cell-derived capped primers (cap snatching). L and S segment-transcribed mRNAs are translated by free ribosomes ( Garcin et al., 1995 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Meier et al., 2021 ). M segment-transcribed mRNA is translated by membrane-bound ribosomes, with the expressed GPC which is likely co-translationally cleaved by cellular proteases to yield G N and G C . The synthesis of the antigenome by L protein serves as a template for genomic RNA replication. Secondary transcription amplifies the synthesis of mRNAs and genome replication. During morphogenesis, G N and G C accumulate in the Golgi apparatus, modified host membranes are acquired, and virions bud into the Golgi. Biology Genus Orthohantavirus includes 38 species for 60 distinct viruses. These viruses and their unclassified, potential relatives, subclinically, and often chronically, infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla, and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents ( Jonsson et al., 2010 , Wu et al., 2018 , Chen et al., 2023 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are overall distributed worldwide, but the individual geographic distribution is dependent on host range. At least some orthohantaviruses may not be as restricted to a particular host as originally thought, but may be carried by animals of multiple hosts ( Goodfellow et al., 2021 , Quizon et al., 2022 , Gu et al., 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease (all in humans) and all disease-causing viruses are rodent-borne. Human infection may occur after inhalation of aerosolized excreta or secreta of infected rodents or direct rodent contact. The two WHO-recognized orthohantavirus-caused diseases are hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), caused by Asian and European viruses (in particular Dobrava virus [DOBV], Hantaan virus [HTNV], Puumala virus [PUUV] and Seoul virus [SEOV]), and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a frequently lethal disease caused by viruses from the Americas (in particular Andes virus [ANDV] and Sin Nombre virus [SNV]) ( Vial et al., 2023 ). The hamster model of wild-type ANDV infection is lethal and largely mimics human HPS ( Hooper et al., 2001 ). After SNV infection in nonhuman primates, some animals develop an HPS-like disease, but cell passage of SNV can result in mutations that render the virus non-pathogenic in this model ( Safronetz et al., 2014 ). Many rodent models result in a chronic, asymptomatic infection, and these have been used in early-stage therapeutic studies ( Strandin et al., 2020 ). However, recent advances have been made in development of an HFRS mouse model using HTNV variants ( Wei et al., 2022 ). Orthohantavirus animal models are reviewed in ( Golden et al., 2015 ). Antigenicity There is considerable serum cross-reactivity between the nucleocapsids of hantavirids, but neutralizing antibodies targeting Gn/Gc are more specific. SNV was first identified as a hantavirid based on cross-reactivity of patient sera with other orthohantavirus antigens ( 1993 ). Similarly, rodents that carried SNV were identified in serosurveys using non-SNV orthohantavirus antigens, since SNV had not been isolated at the time ( Childs et al., 1994 ). Species demarcation criteria Demarcation of species is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Laenen et al., 2019 ). Phylogenetic relationships across the genus have been estimated using maximum likelihood trees generated from complete N, GPC and L amino-acid sequences, and for N and GPC amino-acid sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Hantaviridae ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Hantaviridae (taxid:1980413) VIRION Enveloped, spherical. Diameter from 80 to 120nm. GENOME Segmented Negative-stranded RNA linear genome, L segment is between 6.8 and 12 kb, M segment between 3.2 and 4.9 kb and S segment between 1 and 3 kb. Encodes for four to six proteins. Some hantaviruses also encode a NSs protein on their S segment. GENE EXPRESSION The viral RNA dependent RNA polymerase (L) binds to a promoter on each encapsidated segment, and transcribes the mRNA. These are capped by L protein during synthesis using cap snatching . Transcription is terminated by a strong hairpin sequence at the end of each gene. Puumala virus expressed an additional NSs by leaky scanning in the NS gene. ENZYMES RNA-dependent RNA polymerase L Cap Snatching endonuclease L REPLICATION CYTOPLASMIC Virus attaches to host receptors though Gn-Gc glycoprotein dimer, and is endocytosed into vesicles in the host cell. Fusion of virus membrane with the vesicle membrane; ribonucleocapsid segments are released in the cytoplasm. Transcription , viral mRNAs are capped in the cytoplasm. Replication presumably starts when enough nucleoprotein is present to encapsidate neo-synthetized antigenomes and genomes. The ribonucleocapsids buds at Golgi apparatus, releasing the virion by exocytosis. The hantaviruses (Hantaviridae) ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Back to Andes virus resource There are approximately 92 known viruses in the family Hantaviridae, classified into 52 species. Each species is typically adapted to a specific reservoir host, most commonly rodents, but also bats and moles. With the notable exception of Andes virus, hantaviruses are generally not transmitted from person to person. Based on their geographic distribution, evolutionary relationships, and the diseases they cause in humans, hantaviruses can be broadly divided into three major groups: New World hantaviruses (the Americas) These viruses cause Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a severe respiratory disease. Important examples include Sin Nombre virus and Andes virus. Annual incidence are about 100 cases per year (Andes virus) about 25 cases per year (Sin Nombre virus) Old World hantaviruses (Asia) These viruses are responsible for Hantavirus hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), which is characterized by fever, hemorrhage, and acute kidney injury. Major examples include Hantaan virus and Seoul virus. Annual incidence: more than 10,000 cases worldwide Old World hantaviruses (Europe) European hantaviruses typically cause a milder form of HFRS known as Nephropathia epidemica (NE). The main causative agents are Puumala virus and Dobrava-Belgrade virus. Annual incidence: more than 1,000 cases Together, these viruses represent an important and diverse group of zoonotic pathogens that can cause severe disease following accidental transmission from their natural animal hosts to humans.

papers.title: Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome outbreak linked to cruise ship travel in April-May 2026.
papers.abstract: In April 2026, a hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) outbreak caused by Andes virus (ANDV) occurred on a cruise ship. ANDV genome sequences were obtained for 10 of the 13 identified cases during a cross-country investigation established to share initial raw data for joint analysis with reciprocal quality control. The genomic data, symptom onsets, and plausible contact patterns strongly support a tightly linked outbreak cluster compatible with a single or very few zoonotic spillover events prior to embarkment followed by human-to-human transmission onboard. The outbreak represents the international displacement of a virus already known to be capable, under specific conditions, to transmit among humans, and does not suggest emergence of a unusual viral strain.
authors: International Consortium Investigating the M/V Hondius Outbreak

analysis.summary_en: Background: In April 2026 an HPS outbreak caused by Andes virus occurred on a cruise ship, raising concerns about severe disease and human transmission. Methods: Genome sequences from 10 of 13 cases were obtained during a cross‑country investigation with shared raw data and reciprocal quality control. Results: Genomic, symptom onset, and contact data indicate a tightly linked cluster arising from one or few zoonotic spillovers before embarkation and subsequent human‑to‑human spread onboard. Contribution: The event demonstrates international movement of a known transmissible virus without emergence of a novel strain, informing surveillance and response. Limitations: Only abstract data are provided; detailed study design, sample size, and analytic methods are not reported.

papers.title: Long-term local circulation of an Andes virus lineage in northern Patagonia is linked to the M/V Hondius outbreak.
papers.abstract: In 2026, a hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) outbreak caused by Andes virus (ANDV) occurred on a cruise ship. Analyses revealed an unexpected relationship to an outbreak in Argentina in 2018. Retrospective investigation clarified the 2018 outbreak could involve person-to-person transmission and a common ANDV lineage spanned HPS cases from 2018 to 2025 in a geographically defined area in northern Patagonia, without widespread community transmission of ANDV. Route reconstruction for the index cases in the cruise ship outbreak identified geographically plausible exposures to viruses of this lineage in Argentina, but their timing was inconsistent with the expected ANDV incubation period. The infection source for the cruise ship outbreak cannot be resolved with current information, highlighting the need to expand viral surveillance in the ANDV endemic region.
authors: International Consortium Investigating the M/V Hondius Outbreak

analysis.background: In 2026 a hantavirus pulmonary syndrome outbreak caused by Andes virus occurred on a cruise ship (A1).
analysis.methods: The study performed retrospective and phylogenetic analyses linking the cruise ship cases to earlier cases, but specific design, sample size, and laboratory methods are not reported in the supplied evidence.
analysis.results: Retrospective investigation indicated that the 2018 Argentine outbreak may have involved person‑to‑person transmission and that a single ANDV lineage persisted from 2018 to 2025 in a defined area of northern Patagonia without widespread community spread (A3). Route reconstruction suggested plausible geographic exposures for the cruise ship index cases, yet their timing did not match the expected incubation period (A4).
analysis.contribution: The work highlights the importance of expanding viral surveillance in the Andes virus endemic region to better resolve infection sources (A5).
analysis.limitations: The source of the cruise ship outbreak remains unresolved, and only abstract information is available, limiting detail on methods and data (A5).

analysis_zh.methods: 本研究进行了回顾性和系统发育分析,将邮轮病例与早期病例关联,但供应的证据中未报告具体的研究设计、样本量和实验室方法。
analysis_zh.results: 回顾性调查表明,2018 年阿根廷疫情可能涉及人际传播,且单一的 ANDV 系列从 2018 年持续至 2025 年,在北巴塔哥尼亚的特定区域内存在,但未出现广泛的社区传播 (A3)。路径重建提示邮轮指数病例可能的地理暴露合理,但其时间与预期的潜伏期不符 (A4)。

analysis_zh.limitations: 邮轮疫情的来源仍未确定,且仅有摘要信息可用,限制了对方法和数据的细节了解 (A5)。

papers.title: Immunogenicity of Hantavirus and evaluation of vaccine protective efficacy: A comparative neutralizing antibody study of vaccine strains and representative epidemic strains from selected provinces in China.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) caused by Hantavirus (HV) remains a significant public health burden in the world. HFRS bivalent inactivated vaccine (HFRSbiv) with Hantaan virus (HTNV) and Seoul virus (SEOV) strains isolated 20 years ago have been used in key HFRS endemic provinces in China for HFRS prevention. After decades of effective implementation of comprehensive prevention and control measures, HFRS has entered a stage of epidemic fluctuation at low-level in China. However, the continuous transmission of the virus among rodent host animals may lead to dynamic changes in genetic diversity and immunogenicity of the virus, which may affect the pathogenic mechanism of the virus and the protective effect of vaccines. It is necessary to carry out timely monitoring and evaluation of the immunogenicity of HV. METHODOLOGY/PRINCIPAL FINDINGS: A panel of sera was established by screening serum samples from HFRS patients at convalescent phase and individuals who had received standardized immunization with HFRSbiv. Neutralizing antibody titers against HTNV vaccine strain 84FLi, SEOV vaccine strain L99, and three representative epidemic strains from different genotypes (HTNV: SX26, SEOV: LN03 and FJ-17) were measured using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay-based microneutralization test (MN-ELISA). HV-neutralizing antibodies were detected from all the selected serum samples. Among HFRS patients, 47.92% (23/48) were identified as HTNV infection, 27.08% (13/48) were with SEOV infection, and 25% (12/48) were untypable. There is a significant difference in the titers of neutralizing antibodies against vaccine strains and epidemic strains detected in the serum samples. For HTNV, both patient and vaccinee sera exhibited significantly higher geometric mean titer (GMT) against vaccine strain 84FLi than against epidemic strain SX26 (1:386.08 vs. 1:223.04, P < 0.001; 1:137.94 vs. 1:110.37, P < 0.05, respectively). For SEOV, patient sera showed significantly lower GMT against vaccine strain L99 than against epidemic strain LN03 (1:177.02 vs. 1:297.71, P < 0.01), and vaccinee sera showed significantly lower GMT against L99 than against epidemic strain FJ-17 (1:97.52 vs. 1:243.71, P < 0.001). Significant immunogenicity heterogeneity was observed between SEOV epidemic strains LN03 and FJ-17. CONCLUSIONS/SIGNIFICANCE: The genetic diversity and immunogenicity of HV, which causes HFRS, have certain geographical regional characteristics. The levels of cross neutralizing antibodies induced by infection of HV from different genotypes may vary significantly, but still provide sufficient cross protection. The HFRSbiv currently used in China could induce broad neutralizing antibody, the cross-protective efficacy might vary against different circulating strains and genotypes. It is of great significance to strengthen the monitoring of genetic characteristics of regional specific circulating viral strains, regularly evaluate the matching degree between vaccine protection effectiveness and epidemic strains, predict and evaluate the transmission and pathogenic risks of HV, and timely optimize HFRS prevention and control strategies and measures.

Introduction Several rodent-borne hantaviruses are recognized as important human pathogens causing hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) primarily in Asia and Europe, and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) in the Americas, which are mainly acquired through the inhalation of infectious respiratory particles from rodent urine or feces. The viruses are distributed globally, and approximately 200,000 cases are reported annually, posing a persistent threat to human health [1]. In China, Hantaan virus (HTNV) and Seoul virus (SEOV) are the causative agents of HFRS, and the infection has a relatively wide distribution, with the highest annual reported cases exceeding 110000 in 1980s [2]. Although the annual incidence of HFRS had significantly decreased and maintained a low level in the last two decades, the geographical distribution range of Hantavirus (HV) infection had shown an expanding trend, and the virus presents a more abundant genetic diversity [3]. HV are predominantly hosted by rodents and exhibit strict host specificity, each hantavirus species is primarily carried and transmitted by one or several closely related reservoir hosts [4]. Virus–host adaptive evolution is influenced by ecological environments, host switching events, and gene selection pressures, contributing to the genetic diversity of hantaviruses. Moreover, as segmented RNA viruses, HV possess the capacity for genetic reassortment, enabling the exchange of genomic segments between two parental viruses co-infecting the same cell, thereby generating progeny viruses genetically distinct from both parents [5]. The frequency of segment exchange and the co-infection rate within the same host cell affect the success of genomic reassortment [6]. With the rapid development of laboratory testing technology and the expansion of pathogen monitoring scope, new HV strains continued to be discovered, presenting rich genetic diversity with regional characteristics in China [3,7]. It has been demonstrated that immunization with HFRS bivalent inactivated vaccine (HFRSbiv) which contains HTNV and SEOV, was an effective measure for HFRS prevention. HFRSbiv targeting HTNV and SEOV had been licensed for over two decades. Combined with comprehensive interventions such as immunization, rodent control and environmental sanitation, the disease burden of HFRS in China has been significantly reduced [8,9]. However, the vaccine strains used in China (e.g., HTNV PS-6, SD9805, and SEOV L99, HB9908) were isolated more than 20 years ago. Antigenic variation may exist among different strains within the same serotype, and its impact on vaccine protective efficacy remains unclear. Therefore, evaluating the immunogenicity of regional epidemic HV strains, as well as the immunogenic matching and cross-protection between vaccine strains and currently circulating strains, is practically important. In this study, a serum panel was established using serum samples collected from confirmed HFRS patients and HFRS vaccinees for a comparative analysis of the immunogenicity of HV circulating in China and vaccine strains using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay-based microneutralization test (MN-ELISA). The neutralizing antibody levels against vaccine strains and representative epidemic strains were systematically compared to elucidate immunogenicity differences and to provide experimental evidence for the scientific evaluation of the protective efficacy of HFRS vaccine. Materials and methods Ethics statement This study received ethics approval from the Ethical Committee of National Institute for Viral Disease Control and Prevention, Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants. Study subjects A total of 48 convalescent serum samples from HFRS patients and 28 serum samples from individuals who had completed a three-dose regimen with HFRSbiv were collected between 2019 and 2020 from Heilongjiang Province, which belonged to HFRS national surveillance system. The median interval between disease onset and serum collection for HFRS patients was 14 days, with an interquartile range (IQR) of 10.5 to 19.5 days. Serum samples from vaccinees were collected within one month after the third (booster) dose. HV amplification and titration The HTNV vaccine strain 84FLi, SEOV vaccine strain L99, and previously isolated epidemic strains SX26, LN03, and FJ-17 from HFRS national surveillance system were selected for neutralization assays. All strains were propagated in Vero-E6 cells prior to use. Viral replication was confirmed by quantitative real-time reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) and indirect immunofluorescence assay (IFA). Viral titers were determined by plaque assay. Virus resuscitation, propagation, and identification. HV vaccine strains (84FLi, L99) and epidemic strains (SX26, LN03, FJ-17) were thawed on ice and used to infect Vero-E6 cells. Culture supernatants were collected on day 7 post-infection for HV nucleic acid detection by qRT-PCR. Concurrently, cell antigen slides were prepared for IFA. Plaque assay for viral titration. Vero-E6 cells cultured for 24 h were seeded into 6-well plates and incubated overnight at 37°C with 5% CO2. After forming confluent monolayer, the monolayers were washed, and 500 μL of MEM maintenance medium was added to each well. Serial 10-fold dilutions (10−1 to 10−5) of virus stocks were prepared in MEM, and 500 μL of each dilution was inoculated per well in duplicate. Plates were incubated at 37°C, 5% CO2 for 1.5–2 h for adsorption. After removal of the inoculum, 3 mL of pre-warmed (42°C) agarose overlay (mainly 2 x MEM containing 10% fetal bovine serum,2% Gibco HEPES,1% Penicillin-Streptomycin and 2% low-melting-point agarose) was added per well. Once solidified, plates were inverted and incubated at 37°C, 5% CO2. Seven days later, a second agarose overlay, which was identical to that of the first overlay, with the addition of 3% neutral red to facilitate plaque visualization, was added, and incubation continued for an additional 48–72 h. Plaques were observed and counted. Viral titers were calculated as plaque-forming units per milliliter (PFU/mL): PFU/mL = (average plaque count at a given dilution × reciprocal of dilution) / virus inoculum volume (mL/well). Detection of serum HV IgG antibodies HV IgG antibodies in all serum samples were detected using a commercial HV IgG antibody ELISA kit (Beijing Beier Bioengineering Co., Ltd., enzyme immunoassay). Positive and negative controls were included. All procedures and result interpretation were performed strictly in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions. Neutralizing antibody assay (MN-ELISA) A fixed-virus (100 PFU/0.1 mL) microneutralization assay was employed. Sera were heat-inactivated at 56°C and serially diluted 2-fold in 96-well plates (starting dilution 1:10 for vaccinees and 1:20 for patients, ending at 1:10240), with three replicates per dilution. Each virus strain (84FLi, L99, SX26, LN03, FJ-17) was diluted to working concentration, and 50 μL of virus was mixed with an equal volume of diluted serum. The mixtures were incubated at 37°C, 5% CO2 for 1 h. Subsequently, 100 μL of Vero-E6 cell suspension was added to each well. Virus-positive and cell-negative controls were included. After seven days of incubation at 37°C, 5% CO2, supernatants were discarded, and cells were fixed with cold acetone and inactivated under UV light. After washing, 100 μL of detection antibody mixture (HV monoclonal antibody L13F3 at 1:3200 dilution and HRP-conjugated rabbit anti-mouse IgG at 1:1000 dilution, pre-mixed) was added per well and incubated at 37°C for 45 min. After washing, 100 μL of the mixed TMB substrate solution was added to each well and incubated for 10 min at room temperature in the dark. The reaction was stopped by adding 50 μL of 2 M H2SO4 per well, and the optical density (OD) was measured at 450 nm using a microplate reader. Determination of neutralizing antibody titer and virus typing The neutralizing antibody titer was defined as the highest serum dilution that inhibited 50% of viral infection. The cutoff value (X) for positivity was calculated as: X = [(mean OD of cell-positive controls – mean OD of cell-negative controls)/2) + mean OD of cell-negative controls [10]. Samples with OD values below X were considered positive for neutralization, and the reciprocal of the highest dilution showing positivity was taken as the neutralizing antibody titer. For virus typing, the neutralizing antibody titers against the HTNV vaccine strain 84FLi and the SEOV vaccine strain L99 were compared. If the titer against one type was ≥ 4-fold higher than that against the other, the infection was assigned to that type; otherwise, it was considered untypable. Statistical analysis Raw data were entered, organized, and analyzed using Excel 2019 and GraphPad Prism 10.1.2. Neutralizing antibody titers were expressed as geometric mean titer (GMT). Comparisons among multiple groups were performed using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA). For non-normally distributed data, non-parametric tests (Wilcoxon signed-rank test for two-group comparisons, Friedman test for paired multiple-group comparisons) were applied. A P-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results HV amplification and titer determination To obtain working virus stocks for subsequent neutralization assays, five HV strains (vaccine strains: 84FLi, L99; epidemic strains: SX26, LN03, FJ-17) were resuscitated, propagated, and titrated. All strains replicated efficiently in Vero-E6 cells. On day 7 post-infection, culture supernatants were collected and tested by qRT-PCR, all yielding positive results. IFA revealed typical bright green specific fluorescent granules in infected cells, which were absent in negative control cells, confirming intact viral infectivity (Fig 1). Viral titers were determined by plaque assay. All strains formed classical plaques at a 10−3 dilution (Fig 2). The calculated viral titers (PFU/mL) were as follows: 84FLi, 3.08 × 106; L99, 2.25 × 106; SX26, 5.13 × 105; LN03, 1.23 × 104; FJ-17, 1.65 × 106. These results confirmed successful amplification of all strains for subsequent neutralization assays. Note: The observations were performed at ×200 magnification. (A) 84FLi; (B) L99; (C) SX26; (D) LN03; (E) FJ-17; (F) Negative control. Demographic characteristics and HV typing of HFRS patients Among the 48 HFRS patients, 38 were male and 10 were female, with a median age of 53 years. Farmers accounted for 83.33% (40/48) of the cases; the remaining occupations included three students, one worker, one retiree, and three unemployed/homemakers. Among the 28 vaccinees (11 farmers, 11 students, and 6 teachers), 9 were male and 19 were female, with a median age of 31 years. Sera from HFRS patient and vaccinees were all tested positive for HV IgG antibodies. Based on the typing criteria, of the 48 HFRS patient sera, 23 (47.92%) were identified as HTNV infection, 13 (27.08%) were SEOV infection, and the remaining 12 sera were untypable. Inter-individual variation in neutralizing capacity against HV vaccine and epidemic strains Among the 48 HFRS patient sera, 33 showed higher neutralizing titers against HTNV vaccine strain 84FLi than against epidemic strain SX26, with most differences within 2-fold. Ten sera (20.83%, 10/48) exhibited ≥4-fold higher titers against 84FLi than against SX26. In contrast, neutralizing titers against the SEOV vaccine strain L99 were generally lower than those against the epidemic strain LN03. Nearly half of the sera showed ≥4-fold higher titers against LN03 than against L99. Furthermore, immunogenicity differed between the two SEOV epidemic strains LN03 and FJ-17; 83.33% (40/48) of sera exhibited higher neutralizing titers against LN03 than against FJ-17. Most sera showed low neutralizing titers against FJ-17, with nearly half (43.75%) having titers <1:20 (Fig 3). analysis_zh.background: 肾综合征出血热(肾综合征出血热)由汉坦病毒引起,仍然是全球重要的公共卫生负担。
analysis_zh.methods: 组建了来自康复期肾综合征出血热患者以及接种过双价灭活肾综合征出血热疫苗(HTNV 与 SEOV株,20 年前分离)的受试者血清样本;使用基于 ELISA 的微中和试验(MN‐ELISA)测定针对疫苗株(HTNV 84FLi、SEOV L99)和三株代表性流行株(HTNV SX26、SEOV LN03、FJ‐17)的中和抗体滴度。
analysis_zh.results: 在所有样本中均检测到中和抗体;在 48 例患者中,47.92%(23例)为 HTNV 感染,27.08%(13例)为 SEOV 感染,25%(12例)未分型。针对疫苗株 84FLi 的几何平均滴度(GMT)高于流行株 SX26(1:386.08 对 1:223.04,P<0.001;1:110.37 对 ...,P<0.05)。对于 SEOV,患者血清对疫苗株 L99 的 GMT 低于 LN03(1:177.02 对 1:297.71,P<0.01),且疫苗接种者血清对 L99 的 GMT 低于 FJ‐17(1:97.52 对 1:243.71,P<0.001)。在 SEOV 株 LN03 与 FJ‐17 之间观察到显著的免疫原性异质性。

papers.title: CD8+ regulatory T cells limit immunopathology but impair viral clearance in Hantaan virus infection.
papers.abstract: In hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) caused by Hantaan virus (HTNV), virus-specific CD8+ T cells mediate both viral clearance and immunopathology. Here, we characterized a CD8+ regulatory T cell (Treg) subset restricted by HLA-E (and its murine ortholog Qa-1) in HFRS patients and in a murine HTNV infection model. CD8+ Tregs (CD122+Eomes+CD49dloKIR+), a subset substantially enriched for HLA-E-restricted T cells, were significantly reduced in peripheral blood of HFRS patients and displayed a terminally differentiated profile with elevated expression of KLRG-1, NKG2A, CTLA-4, and Fas-L, correlating with disease severity. Two HTNV glycoprotein-derived nonapeptides that bound Qa-1 were identified. Following immunization with the identified HTNV peptides and subsequent HTNV challenge, wild-type (WT) mice showed attenuated renal immunopathology, whereas D227K knock-in mice (with disrupted Qa-1-CD8/TCR interaction) showed enhanced viral clearance in the spleen and kidney but exacerbated renal immunopathology. Mechanistically, Qa-1-restricted CD8+ Tregs from WT mice suppressed effector CD8+ T cell proliferation in a peptide-specific, CD8/TCR-dependent manner via enhanced TGF-β secretion. Strikingly, D227K mutation dichotomously reshaped Treg phenotype: bulk polyclonal CD8+ Tregs displayed compensatory upregulation of inhibitory receptors (NKG2A, CTLA-4, PD-1) and TGF-β, whereas epitope-specific CD8+ Tregs showed impaired antigen-specific suppressive function and attenuated TGF-β production. Collectively, these findings indicate that HLA-E/Qa-1-restricted CD8+ Tregs can restrain immunopathology during HTNV infection, potentially at the cost of delayed viral elimination. Modulation of this axis may provide insights for therapeutic strategies in HFRS and related viral hemorrhagic fevers.

analysis.summary_en: Background: CD8+ T cells drive both viral clearance and immunopathology in hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome caused by Hantaan virus. analysis_zh.methods: 作者在肾综合征出血热患者及小鼠HTNV感染模型中,鉴定了受HLA‐E(及其小鼠同源Qa‐1)限制的CD8+调节性T细胞(Treg)亚群。
analysis_zh.results: 在肾综合征出血热患者外周血中,CD8+ Tregs(CD122+Eomes+CD49dloKIR+)显著减少,并呈现终末分化表型,KLRG‐1、NKG2A、CTLA‐4和Fas‐L表达升高,且与疾病严重程度相关;鉴定出两种能够结合Qa‐1的HTNV糖蛋白来源的九肽;用这些肽免疫可减轻野生型小鼠的肾免疫病理,但D227K敲入小鼠虽显示病毒清除增强,却导致肾病理加重;Qa‐1限制的CD8+ Tregs通过提升TGF‐β分泌,以肽特异性、CD8/TCR依赖的方式抑制效应CD8+细胞增殖;D227K突变重塑了Treg表型,使整体细胞上抑制受体和TGF‐β上调,但削弱了抗原特异性抑制功能。
analysis_zh.contribution: 这些结果表明,HLA‐E/Qa‐1限制的CD8+ Tregs能够在HTNV感染期间抑制免疫病理,可能以延迟病毒清除为代价,并提示调控该通路或可为肾综合征出血热及相关病毒性出血热的治疗策略提供依据。
analysis_zh.limitations: 仅提供了摘要数据,未报告详细方法、样本量、统计分析及更广泛的背景信息。

papers.full_text: Disclaimer: Early release articles are not considered as final versions. Any changes will be reflected in the online version in the month the article is officially released. Volume 32, Number 12—December 2026 Dispatch Rat Hepatitis E Virus and Seoul Hantavirus in Pet Rats, Germany Suggested citation for this article Abstract Pet rats represent a reservoir of multiple zoonotic pathogens. We demonstrated that pet rats, previously confirmed to be Seoul orthohantavirus–infected and involved in human infections in Germany, were concurrently infected with rat hepatitis E virus. The high degree of rat hepatitis E virus sequence identity suggests a single incursion event. Despite being closely associated with human settlements for much of recent human history, brown rats (Rattus norvegicus) were not domesticated as pets until the 17th and 18th Centuries in Japan (1). Wild brown rats, which are prolific synanthropic pests, harbor a great diversity of zoonotic agents (2,3). Pet rats, the domesticated form of brown rats, have likewise been associated with outbreaks of Leptospira spp. (4), Seoul virus (SEOV; Orthohantavirus seoulense) (5), and cowpox virus (6). SEOV is a zoonotic hantavirus found in both wild and pet rats globally (7). In Germany, pet rats have been linked to 4 detections of cases of human SEOV infection (5,8,9). Additional zoonotic pathogens in wild rats include the human pathogenic hepatitis E virus (HEV; Paslahepevirus balayani) and rat hepatitis E virus (rHEV; Rocahepevirus ratti). HEV is one of the main causative agents of acute hepatitis in humans worldwide and is typically transmitted through the fecal–oral route, consumption of undercooked pork, or blood and organ transplants. rHEV has been detected in wild brown rats and black rats (Rattus rattus) worldwide and is now recognized as a novel human pathogen causing acute and chronic hepatitis (10,11). Rats (Rattus spp.) are reservoirs of rHEV but have also been reported to be incidentally infected with genotype HEV-3 (12). To assess the presence of rHEV, HEV-3, and other related hepeviruses, as well as potential co-infection with SEOV and tissue distribution of hepevirus RNA and SEOV antigen in SEOV-infected and noninfected pet rats, we screened samples from 13 pet rats associated with 3 SEOV detections in human patients in Germany by molecular and serologic assays. Of those 13 pet rats, 11 tested positive for SEOV RNA in previous studies (5,9) (Appendix Table 1). We extracted RNA from liver tissue and screened it by a nested broad-spectrum reverse transcription PCR (RT-PCR) capable of detecting multiple HEV genotypes and rHEV (Appendix). By sequencing the RT-PCR products, we identified rHEV RNA in 3 of the 13 pet rats (KS19/1354, KS19/2196, and KS22/001), a finding further confirmed by rHEV-specific real-time RT-PCR (Appendix Table 1). The 3 pet rats, which were previously shown to be infected by SEOV (Appendix Table 1), came from 3 different owners; 2 rats were obtained from the same vendor and the source for the third rat was unknown (5,8,9). The 276 nt-long open reading frame (ORF) 1 and corresponding amino acid (aa) sequences of rHEV from the 3 pet rats were nearly identical (99.15%–100%) (Appendix Table 2). For further sequence comparisons and phylogenetic analyses, we downloaded 91 partial and 60 complete genome rHEV sequences from GenBank (Figure). In addition, we determined short ORF1 sequences of 12 wild brown rats from Rotterdam (n = 8) and Amsterdam (n = 4) (the Netherlands) that previously tested positive for rHEV RNA (2). Phylogenetic analysis demonstrated that the 3 pet rat–derived sequences were highly similar (98.55%–98.91%) to a wild rat–derived rHEV sequence from Rotterdam (M226) (Figure, panel A). A multiplex serology approach using bead-based Luminex technology (R&D Systems, https://www.rndsystems.com) (Appendix) detected rHEV-reactive antibodies in 12 of 13 pet rat blood samples; 3 of those 12 samples also showed reactivity to HEV-3 antigen (Appendix Table 1). Subsequent Western blot analysis using the same 2 antigens mainly supported multiplex serology results: 11 of 12 multiplex serology–positive samples also tested positive for rHEV. Of the 11 seropositive samples, 10 also reacted in the Western blot assay with the HEV-3 antigen (Appendix Table 1, Figure 1). That high seroprevalence suggests widespread circulation in pet rat breeding facilities, which should be confirmed using a larger sample size. In all 3 rHEV RNA–positive pet rats, rHEV-reactive antibodies were detected by multiplex serology. Differences in the results of multiplex serology and Western blot assay can be explained by differences in the epitope presentation and sensitivity of both assays. We obtained near-full rHEV genome sequences from the 3 pet rats from Germany (KS19/1354, KS19/2196, and KS22/001) and from 3 of the wild brown rats from the Netherlands by using a combination of high-throughput sequencing and RT-PCR–based sequence determination of the hypervariable genome region. The wild brown rats (M226, M268, and M186) from Rotterdam were selected for different levels of ORF1 sequence similarity to the 3 pet rat–derived sequences (Figure, panel A). The rHEV full genome sequences from the 3 pet rats were >99.7% identical, and nucleotide and amino acid sequences of all 4 ORFs and encoded proteins were >99.2% identical (Appendix Table 2). As in ORF1, the full genomes from the 3 German pet rats were most similar to the sequence from wild brown rat M226 from Rotterdam (full sequence >99.2% identical; each ORF >98.3%) (Appendix Table 3) and clustered with that sequence in the phylogeny (Figure, panel B). The most closely related rHEV sequences from Germany were detected in wild brown rats from Hamburg (Figure, panel B). The only sequence from a human patient in Germany (13) clustered among sequences from wild brown rats from Berlin, separate from the pet rat sequences (Figure, panel B; Appendix Table 3). On the basis of the complete coding sequences of pet rat–derived rHEV, we selected probe sequences to detect rHEV RNA through in situ hybridization in formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissues of the pet rats mounted on adhesive microscope slides (Appendix). We clearly detected a disseminated in situ hybridization signal using brightfield microscopy in the livers (hepatocytes) of rats KS19/1354, KS19/2196, and KS22/001, confirming the rHEV quantitative RT-PCR results (Appendix Table 1, Figure 2). In addition, we detected an oligofocal in situ hybridization signal in the spleen of pet rat KS22/001 and in the intestinal lumen of pet rat KS19/1354. We detected no signal in the other tissues tested (Appendix Table 4). Nucleocapsid protein immunohistochemistry analysis of the rHEV-SEOV coinfected pet rats KS19/1354, KS19/2196, and KS22/001 demonstrated SEOV antigen in multiple organs, predominantly the kidney and brain; antigen was detected less frequently in the spleen, intestine, liver, and lung (Appendix Tables 1, 3, Figure 2). That distribution is consistent with the previously described widespread endothelial tropism of SEOV in naturally infected wild rats and experimentally infected laboratory rats (14). In our study, advanced autolysis limited the assessment of pathological changes. We could not assess colocalization of both viruses because of insufficient tissue material. The co-infection of pet rats with the zoonotic pathogens SEOV and ratHEV and the rat-to-human transmission of SEOV in those cases (8,9) highlights a public health concern posed by pet rats. Unfortunately, the owners of the pet rats did not consent to providing blood samples; therefore, their rHEV serologic status could not be assessed. The near-identical rHEV sequences in the pet rats indicate a single incursion event consistent with potentially being independently obtained from the same vendor in Germany (5). The close similarity between the pet rat rHEV sequences and a wild rat–derived sequence from the Netherlands might indicate a wild rat origin of pet rat rHEV, further circulation by pet rat trade, and (at least mostly) uncoupled dynamics of rHEV in wild and captive rats. Owners and general practitioners should be aware of potential zoonotic risks associated with pet rats so that preventive hygienic measures can be taken and correct diagnosis supported. His research interests include the interplay between pathogen and host ecology, with a focus on small mammals. papers.title: An NCG mouse model of Hantaan virus reveals systemic infection and organ-specific cellular tropism.
papers.abstract: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) caused by Hantaan virus (HTNV) is primarily endemic across Eurasia, posing a severe threat of renal failure and mortality. The mechanisms of HTNV infection remain poorly understood, largely due to the lack of susceptible animal models. In this study, we established a systemic HTNV infection mouse model using highly immunodeficient NCG mice. Following viral inoculation, we assessed viral loads via quantitative RT-PCR and mapped cellular tropism and co-localization of HTNV with potential receptors using immunofluorescence staining. While histopathological lesions were subclinical, HTNV-infected NCG mice exhibited robust viremia and sustained viral replication across multiple organs, including the kidney, lung, spleen, reproductive organs, and liver. HTNV exhibited distinct organ-specific cellular tropism in vivo, predominantly targeting fibroblasts and interstitial cells of the renal collecting duct in the kidney, alveolar epithelial cells and macrophages in the lung, and broadly infecting multiple cell populations in the brain and ovary. Co-localization analyses indicated HTNV infection might be associated with distinct entry receptors across target organs: potentially ITGB1 and gC1qR in specific renal cells, and ITGB1 and ITGB2 in pulmonary AT1 cells and macrophages, respectively. These findings demonstrate that NCG mouse is a valuable in vivo model for studying HTNV replication and systemic dissemination.

source_records.abstract: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) caused by Hantaan virus (HTNV) is primarily endemic across Eurasia, posing a severe threat of renal failure and mortality. The mechanisms of HTNV infection remain poorly understood, largely due to the lack of susceptible animal models. In this study, we established a systemic HTNV infection mouse model using highly immunodeficient NCG mice. Following viral inoculation, we assessed viral loads via quantitative RT-PCR and mapped cellular tropism and co-localization of HTNV with potential receptors using immunofluorescence staining. While histopathological lesions were subclinical, HTNV-infected NCG mice exhibited robust viremia and sustained viral replication across multiple organs, including the kidney, lung, spleen, reproductive organs, and liver. HTNV exhibited distinct organ-specific cellular tropism in vivo, predominantly targeting fibroblasts and interstitial cells of the renal collecting duct in the kidney, alveolar epithelial cells and macrophages in the lung, and broadly infecting multiple cell populations in the brain and ovary. Co-localization analyses indicated HTNV infection might be associated with distinct entry receptors across target organs: potentially ITGB1 and gC1qR in specific renal cells, and ITGB1 and ITGB2 in pulmonary AT1 cells and macrophages, respectively. These findings demonstrate that NCG mouse is a valuable in vivo model for studying HTNV replication and systemic dissemination.

analysis.summary_en: Background: HFRS caused by Hantaan virus is endemic across Eurasia and can lead to renal failure and death. Methods: Researchers used highly immunodeficient NCG mice to create a systemic HTNV infection model, measuring viral loads by quantitative RT‑PCR and mapping cellular tropism and receptor co‑localization with immunofluorescence. Results: Infected NCG mice showed robust viremia and sustained replication in multiple organs, with organ‑specific tropism to fibroblasts/interstitial cells in kidney, alveolar epithelial cells/macrophages in lung, and diverse brain/ovary cells; co‑localization suggested ITGB1, gC1qR, and ITGB2 as possible entry receptors. papers.title_zh: 一种针对 汉滩病毒 的NCG小鼠模型揭示了系统性感染和器官特异性细胞嗜性。

analysis_zh.background: 肾综合征出血热 由 汉滩病毒 引起,流行于欧亚大陆,构成严重的肾功能衰竭和死亡威胁。
analysis_zh.methods: 本研究利用高度免疫缺陷的 NCG 小鼠建立了系统性 HTNV 感染模型,并通过定量 RT‐PCR 评估病毒载量,同时使用免疫荧光染色绘制细胞嗜性及受体共定位图谱。
analysis_zh.results: HTNV 感染的 NCG 小鼠出现强烈的血病毒症,并在肾、肺、脾、生殖器官和肝脏中持续复制;病毒表现出器官特异性细胞嗜性——肾集合管的成纤维细胞和间质细胞、肺的肺泡上皮细胞和巨噬细胞,以及多种脑部和卵巢细胞群;共定位分析提示 ITGB1、gC1qR 和 ITGB2 可能作为不同器官的进入受体。
analysis_zh.contribution: 这些发现表明 NCG 小鼠是研究 HTNV 复制和系统性传播的有价值的体内模型。
analysis_zh.limitations: 仅有摘要信息,未提供详细的定量数据、样本量和实验条件。

papers.title: Molecular evolution of Andes virus lineages leading to recent human outbreaks
papers.abstract: Abstract Andes virus (ANDV) is exceptional among hantaviruses in its capacity for person-to-person transmission, but whether outbreaks reflect recent viral adaptation or emergence of pre-existing reservoir lineages remains unclear. We generated paired blood- and nasal-derived genomes from the MV Hondius outbreak and integrated them with a segment-linked collection of human- and rodent-derived ANDV sequences, including incomplete genomes. We developed a linkage-informed missing-segment framework that preserves isolate identity, sampling time, and cross-segment placement without imputing nucleotide states, enabling sensitivity analyses of patchy segment coverage. Across five human outbreaks, dated phylogenies placed outbreak lineages independently within geographically structured reservoir diversity, with closest sampled ancestry predating detection. Time-dependent-rate analyses indicated a deeper reservoir-associated history, while mutation reconstruction, selection tests, branch-rate comparisons, and structural mapping found no recurrent adaptive transition preceding human transmission. MV Hondius samples showed minimal consensus-level diversification. These results shift attention from repeated recent adaptation toward deeper lineage properties and ecological opportunity.

papers.title_zh: 近期人类暴发相关的安第斯病毒谱系的分子进化

analysis_zh.background: 安第斯病毒 (安第斯病毒) 仅在人类之间传播,但尚不清楚近期爆发是由新的病毒适应还是由先前存在的宿主种群谱系出现所驱动 (A1).
analysis_zh.methods: 作者从2026年MV Hondius爆发中生成了血液和鼻腔来源的S、M、L片段基因组,并将其与一组与片段相关联的人类和啮齿类来源的安第斯病毒序列(包括不完整基因组)结合 (A2)。他们采用了基于连锁信息的缺失片段框架,保留了分离株身份、采样时间和跨片段定位,而不进行核苷酸插补 (A3).
analysis_zh.results: 时间校准的系统发育图将五个人体爆发谱系独立定位于地理结构化的宿主多样性中,最近的采样祖先早于检测时间 (A4)。时间依赖速率分析揭示更深层的宿主历史,突变重建、选择检验、分支速率比较和结构映射均未发现在人类传播前的反复适应转变 (A5)。MV Hondius 样本显示一致性水平的变异极小 (A6).
analysis_zh.contribution: 本研究将关注点从反复的近期适应转向更深层谱系特性和生态机会,作为安第斯病毒爆发的驱动因素 (A7).
analysis_zh.limitations: 该分析依赖稀疏且采样不均的基因组数据,许多分离株缺乏完整片段集,可能导致系统发育和速率估计偏差 (F28‐F31)。此外,该工作为预印本,尚未经过同行评议 (F15).

analysis.background: The review addresses the need to synthesize mathematical modeling studies of hantavirus spillover to inform One Health and surveillance strategies.
analysis.main_directions: It catalogs environmental drivers, model structures, and surveillance-readiness gaps, providing reproducible code and data for future work.
analysis.current_state: Current knowledge is fragmented, with diverse modeling approaches but limited integration of ecological, epidemiological, and surveillance data.
analysis.gaps: Key gaps include insufficient data on host–environment interactions, lack of standardized modeling frameworks, and limited evidence on surveillance readiness.
analysis.future_research: Future work should develop unified, data‑rich models, validate them across regions, and embed them in real‑time surveillance systems to improve spillover prediction and preparedness.

papers.title: Progress in antiviral and vaccine strategies against hantavirus: Current advances and future perspectives
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses are rodent-associated zoonotic RNA viruses responsible for hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), two clinically distinct diseases characterized by vascular dysfunction and potentially severe organ failure. Their geographic distribution, antigenic diversity, and variable clinical outcomes complicate the development of broadly applicable medical countermeasures. The aim of this narrative review is to critically examine the molecular rationale, current evidence, and translational readiness of antiviral and vaccine strategies against hantavirus infections. Antiviral approaches include ribavirin, favipiravir, RNA interference, neutralizing monoclonal antibodies, and investigational host-directed therapies, with particular attention to differences between human clinical evidence and findings from cell culture or animal models. Vaccine strategies are evaluated across regionally implemented inactivated vaccines, DNA candidates assessed in early-phase human trials, and recombinant protein, viral vector, and messenger RNA platforms that remain predominantly preclinical. The review also distinguishes vaccine immunogenicity, experimental protection, durability of immune responses, and clinical effectiveness. Major barriers to translation include virus-specific therapeutic responses, narrow treatment windows, targeted delivery, antigenic diversity, and the absence of validated correlates of protective immunity. This review highlights the experimental and clinical evidence needed to advance promising antiviral and vaccine candidates toward effective strategies for prevention and treatment of hantavirus infections.

Narra Review 2026; 2 (3): e43 - http://doi.org/10.52225/narrarev.v2i3.43 Page 2 of 23 Narrative Review Introduction Hantaviruses are enveloped, tripartite, negative-sense RNA viruses within the family Hantaviridae. The genome comprises small (S), medium (M), and large (L) segments that encode proteins required for viral replication and host-cell entry [1]. Rodents are the principal reservoirs of human-pathogenic hantaviruses, and their distribution and transmission are shaped by reservoir ecology and environmental conditions [2]. Ecological analyses based largely on Chinese surveillance further emphasize that environmental variability and host population dynamics can influence hantavirus transmission [3]. Human infection is associated primarily with two major clinical syndromes: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), most commonly reported in Asia and Europe, and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), predominantly reported in the Americas [4,5]. HFRS is characterized by fever, vascular instability, hemorrhagic manifestations, and varying degrees of acute kidney injury [4]. In contrast, HCPS may progress rapidly to noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, respiratory failure, and circulatory shock [5]. These geographic patterns are associated with differences in circulating viral species and their reservoir hosts. Moreover, changes in land use, land cover, and human–rodent interactions may further modify exposure risks [6-8]. Human infection usually follows inhalation of aerosols contaminated with urine, feces, or saliva from infected rodents, particularly during activities that disturb contaminated materials [9]. Epidemiological investigations have identified residential, occupational, and recreational exposures among patients with HCPS in the United States [10]. Human-to-human transmission is uncommon but has been documented for Andes virus, typically in circumstances involving close or prolonged contact [9,11]. Accordingly, current prevention strategies primarily focus on reducing human exposure to infected rodents and their excreta, particularly in potentially contaminated residential and occupational environments [12]. Vascular endothelial cells are major targets of pathogenic hantaviruses, and clinically significant vascular leakage can develop without extensive direct virus-mediated cytolysis [13]. Altered vascular endothelial growth factor signaling has been implicated in endothelial barrier integrity in experimental systems [14]. Innate and adaptive immune responses contribute to viral control but may also exacerbate inflammation and vascular dysfunction, suggesting that therapeutic strategies may need to address both viral replication and dysregulated host responses [15,16]. Recent surveillance data illustrate the continuing, geographically heterogeneous disease burden. In China, national surveillance recorded 3,271 cases of epidemic hemorrhagic fever and 16 deaths in 2025 [17]. In the European Union/European Economic Area (EU/EEA), 1,885 hantavirus infections were reported in 2023, corresponding to a notification rate of 0.4 cases per 100,000 population [18]. In the Americas, the Pan American Health Organization reported 229 confirmed cases of hantavirus pulmonary syndrome and 59 deaths through epidemiological week 47 of 2025, corresponding to a reported case-fatality proportion of 25.7% [19]. These figures originate from different years, surveillance systems, and case definitions and should not be interpreted as directly comparable estimates of regional incidence or disease lethality. Despite this burden, supportive management remains the cornerstone of clinical care, and no antiviral has demonstrated consistent efficacy across HFRS and HCPS [9]. A randomized clinical trial conducted in China reported reduced mortality and selected complications among patients with HFRS receiving intravenous ribavirin [20]. However, a placebo-controlled trial in HCPS did not establish a clinical benefit during the cardiopulmonary phase, underscoring why treatment findings cannot be generalized across syndromes or disease stages [21]. Favipiravir has shown antiviral activity and improved survival under selected preclinical conditions [22]. RNA interference has suppressed Andes virus replication in cultured cells [23]. Neutralizing monoclonal antibodies have conferred protection in selected animal challenge models, but their efficacy in patients remains unconfirmed [24]. Collectively, these findings illustrate the different levels of evidence supporting current antiviral candidates, ranging from clinical investigation to in vitro and animal-model studies [25]. Prevention faces similar translational challenges. Inactivated vaccines targeting HFRS- associated hantaviruses have been implemented in China [26], while Hantavax is an authorized Khairullah et al. Narra Review 2026; 2 (3): e43 - http://doi.org/10.52225/narrarev.v2i3.43 Page 3 of 23 Narrative Review inactivated Hantaan virus vaccine in South Korea [27]. In contrast, a bivalent Hantaan/Puumala DNA vaccine has reached phase IIa clinical evaluation for safety and immunogenicity, without demonstrating clinical effectiveness against naturally acquired infection [28]. Recombinant protein, viral vector-based, and messenger RNA vaccine platforms have been investigated predominantly in preclinical studies, and the breadth and durability of vaccine-induced protection remain important evidence gaps [29]. Accordingly, the aim of this narrative review is to critically evaluate the molecular rationale, evidence levels, and translational limitations of current hantavirus antiviral and vaccine strategies. The discussion first summarizes mechanisms relevant to therapeutic targeting and antigen design, then compares clinically investigated interventions with preclinical and exploratory approaches, assesses the development status of vaccine platforms, and identifies priorities for further experimental and clinical validation. Virology and pathogenesis of hantavirus Genome organization and viral structure The hantavirus genome comprises three RNA segments, each encoding proteins with distinct roles in the viral life cycle. The S segment encodes the nucleocapsid (N) protein, which encapsidates viral RNA and participates in viral RNA synthesis [1]. The M segment encodes a glycoprotein precursor processed into the surface glycoproteins Gn and Gc, which mediate viral attachment and membrane fusion [30]. Because Gn and Gc contain neutralizing antibody epitopes, they represent important targets for antibody-based interventions and vaccine antigen design [31−33]. Furthermore, the ability of Gn and Gc to self-assemble into virus-like particles in experimental expression systems provides a potential platform for vaccine antigen presentation [34]. The L segment encodes the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp), which is responsible for viral messenger RNA (mRNA) transcription and genome replication [1]. During transcription, the viral transcription machinery uses short capped RNA primers acquired from host transcripts through cap-snatching to synthesize mRNA from negative-sense genomic RNA (vRNA) [35]. In contrast, genome replication proceeds through primer-independent synthesis of a full-length positive-sense complementary RNA (cRNA), or antigenome, from the vRNA template [36]. The antigenome subsequently serves as an intermediate template for producing new negative-sense genomic RNA, rather than functioning as a protein-coding transcript [37]. These mechanistically distinct steps identify RdRp and viral RNA synthesis as relevant targets for direct-acting antivirals. In addition, experimental evidence demonstrating interactions between N and RdRp highlights the importance of the viral replication complex in RNA synthesis [38]. Viral entry and host interaction Hantavirus entry begins with Gn/Gc-mediated interactions with host-cell entry factors, followed by endocytosis and membrane fusion within endosomal compartments [13,30]. Earlier cell-based studies implicated αvβ3 integrins in entry by certain HFRS-associated hantaviruses [39]. In contrast, protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) has been experimentally identified as a critical entry factor for Andes virus and Sin Nombre virus in pulmonary endothelial cells. Disruption of PCDH1 expression also conferred protection against Andes virus challenge in hamsters [40]. These findings indicate that entry-factor dependence differs among hantaviruses and should not be represented as a single universal receptor pathway. For Hantaan virus, clathrin-dependent receptor-mediated endocytosis was demonstrated in a cell-based investigation, although this pathway should not be assumed to operate identically in all hantaviruses [41]. Gn and Gc contribute complementary functions to viral attachment, membrane fusion, and virion assembly [42]. Following entry, pathogenic hantaviruses primarily target vascular endothelial cells, where infection can impair barrier function without extensive direct viral cytolysis [13]. Experimental studies have linked enhanced vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) signaling to increased endothelial permeability [14]. Specifically, Andes virus infection of human lung endothelial cells has been associated with increased VEGF production and reduced junctional VE-cadherin, Khairullah et al. Narra Review 2026; 2 (3): e43 - http://doi.org/10.52225/narrarev.v2i3.43 Page 4 of 23 Narrative Review contributing to endothelial barrier disruption [43]. The resulting vascular leakage contributes to renal involvement in HFRS and pulmonary and cardiovascular complications in HCPS [4, 5, 44]. Furthermore, pathogenic hantaviruses have been shown to promote platelet adherence to infected endothelial cells in experimental systems, suggesting an additional mechanism contributing to vascular dysfunction [45]. The connections between viral entry, endothelial dysfunction, and organ involvement are summarized in Figure 1. Figure 1. Hantavirus structure, entry, and endothelial pathogenesis. Immunopathogenesis Host immune responses contribute to both control of hantavirus infection and the development of vascular injury. Innate recognition involving retinoic acid-inducible gene I (RIG-I)-like receptors activates type I interferon signaling and restricts Hantaan virus replication in experimental systems [46]. However, hantaviruses can modulate these antiviral pathways, and the outcome reflects interactions between viral replication and host immune regulation [37]. In a Hantaan virus model, viral interference with TRIM25-associated RIG-I-like receptor signaling was reported as a mechanism of innate immune antagonism [47]. Clinical observations in patients with Puumala virus infection further demonstrate the involvement of both innate and adaptive immune responses during hantavirus infection [48]. In addition, neutralizing antibodies targeting the Gn/Gc glycoproteins can inhibit viral entry and represent important components of vaccine development and passive immunotherapy, although their protective breadth varies depending on the antibody and viral species [24,31]. Adaptive immune responses, particularly virus-specific T-cell responses, may contribute to viral control but can also participate in immunopathology. In an endothelial-cell culture model, hantavirus-specific cytotoxic T lymphocytes increased permeability of infected endothelial monolayers, suggesting a potential mechanism of immune-mediated endothelial injury [49]. However, the extent to which this experimental mechanism contributes to vascular pathology in patients remains incompletely established. Dysregulated inflammatory mediators and VEGF- associated signaling may further impair endothelial junctions and amplify vascular leakage [14,15, 50]. These findings highlight the need to distinguish protective antiviral immunity from potentially harmful immune-mediated responses and support the investigation of Khairullah et al. Current antiviral strategies against hantavirus Current management of hantavirus infection relies primarily on supportive and organ-directed care, including respiratory and hemodynamic support and renal replacement therapy when clinically indicated [9]. Although several antiviral candidates have been investigated, their levels of supporting evidence and clinical development vary substantially. Ribavirin has undergone human clinical testing, with different outcomes reported between HFRS and HCPS [20,21]. In contrast, favipiravir [22], RNA interference-based approaches [23], and neutralizing monoclonal antibodies [24] remain supported predominantly by preclinical evidence from cell-based and animal studies. Additional compounds identified through cell-based screening have demonstrated potential to interfere with hantavirus entry, although their therapeutic relevance remains to be established [51]. Their geographic distribution, antigenic diversity, and variable clinical outcomes complicate the development of broadly applicable medical countermeasures. The aim of this narrative review is to critically examine the molecular rationale, current evidence, and translational readiness of antiviral and vaccine strategies against hantavirus infections. Antiviral approaches include ribavirin, favipiravir, RNA interference, neutralizing monoclonal antibodies, and investigational host-directed therapies, with particular attention to differences between human clinical evidence and findings from cell culture or animal models. Vaccine strategies are evaluated across regionally implemented inactivated vaccines, live-attenuated vaccines, DNA candidates assessed in early-phase human trials, recombinant protein, viral vector, and messenger RNA platforms that remain predominantly preclinical. The genome comprises small (S), medium (M), and large (L) segments that encode proteins required for viral replication and host-cell entry [1]. Rodents are the principal reservoirs of human-pathogenic hantaviruses, and their distribution and transmission are shaped by reservoir ecology and environmental conditions [2]. Ecological analyses based largely on Chinese surveillance further emphasize that environmental variability and host population dynamics can influence hantavirus transmission [3]. Human infection is associated primarily with two major clinical syndromes: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), most commonly reported in Asia and Europe, and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), predominantly reported in the Americas [4,5]. HFRS is characterized by fever, vascular instability, hemorrhagic manifestations, and varying degrees of acute kidney injury [4]. In contrast, HCPS may progress rapidly to noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, respiratory failure, and circulatory shock [5]. These geographic patterns are associated with differences in circulating viral species and their reservoir hosts. Moreover, changes in land use, land cover, and human–rodent interactions may further modify exposure risks [6-8]. Human infection usually follows inhalation of aerosols contaminated with urine, feces, or saliva from infected rodents, particularly during activities that disturb contaminated materials [9]. Epidemiological investigations have identified residential, occupational, and recreational exposures among patients with HCPS in the United States [10]. Human-to-human transmission is uncommon but has been documented for Andes virus, typically in circumstances involving close or prolonged contact [9,11]. Accordingly, current prevention strategies primarily focus on reducing human exposure to infected rodents and their excreta, particularly in potentially contaminated residential and occupational environments [12]. Vascular endothelial cells are major targets of pathogenic hantaviruses, and clinically significant vascular leakage can develop without extensive direct virus-mediated cytolysis [13]. Altered vascular endothelial growth factor signaling has been implicated in endothelial barrier integrity in experimental systems [14]. Innate and adaptive immune responses contribute to viral control but may also exacerbate inflammation and vascular dysfunction, suggesting that therapeutic strategies may need to address both viral replication and dysregulated host responses [15,16]. analysis.main_directions: The review discusses antiviral modalities—ribavirin, favipiravir, RNAi, monoclonal antibodies, and host‑directed therapies (A4)—and vaccine platforms ranging from regionally used inactivated vaccines to DNA, recombinant protein, viral‑vector, and mRNA candidates (A5).
